text: Before anyone enters a confined space or a live sewer or water structure (lift station wet well, valve or meter vault, manhole on a live line, tank, large pipe), stop and isolate everything that could start, flow, fill, pressurize or move while people are inside. In plain steps: 1) List every source: pumps and their floats or automatic start, force mains and check valves, gravity flow from upstream, bypass pumps, water or air lines, mixers and gates, electrical feeds, and water or pressure held behind a valve or plug. 2) Shut each one down the normal way. 3) Isolate it so it cannot come back on: open the disconnect and lock it (a control switch or float is not isolation); close valves and lock or tag them; for a line that could flood or gas the space, blank it, remove a section, or use double block and bleed (two closed valves locked or tagged, with the drain or vent between them open). 4) Release stored energy: bleed pressure, drain, block anything that can drop or turn. 5) Verify before entry: try to start the pump from its controls and confirm no pressure or flow. A lock physically stops a restart; a tag is only a warning. Good practice is a personal lock for each person going in, removed only by that person when they are out. A live sewer usually cannot be fully shut off upstream, so plugs, bypass, continuous air monitoring and a flow and weather watch are part of the plan. The entry permit lists the isolation used and the entry supervisor checks it before signing. Many owners and utilities operate their own valves and pumps: get their lockout done and confirmed. Plain-language guidance: your company program, the owner's procedure and the regulation govern.
title: Lockout before entry: isolate pumps, lines and power before anyone goes into a wet well, vault, manhole or live structure
topic: Lockout and isolation before entering a confined space or a live sewer or water structure
source: 29 CFR 1926.1202 (isolation, blanking, double block and bleed); 1926.1204(c)(3) and (e)(1); 1910.146(d)(3)(iii) and (f)(8); 1910.147(d); 1910.146 Appendix E

text: Construction crews entering a permit space work under 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA. The permit space program must include "isolating the permit space and physical hazard(s) within the space" (1926.1204(c)(3)). Isolation means entrants are completely protected against the release of energy and material into the space and contact with a physical hazard, by blanking or blinding, misaligning or removing sections of lines, pipes or ducts, a double block and bleed system, lockout or tagout of all sources of energy, blocking or disconnecting mechanical linkages, or barriers (1926.1202). Forced-air ventilation does not count as eliminating or isolating a hazard (1926.1203(g)), and alternate (ventilation-only) entry needs all physical hazards eliminated or isolated first (1926.1203(e)(1)). A plant's or utility's own staff (general industry) follow 1910.146: "isolating the permit space" (1910.146(d)(3)(iii)), with the isolation measures written on the permit (1910.146(f)(8)). OSHA's lockout/tagout standard 1910.147 (shutdown, isolation, lock or tag, stored energy, verify isolation) covers servicing and maintenance in general industry, not construction (1910.147(a)(1)(ii)(A)); on a construction job the electrical rule is 1926.417: deenergized equipment or circuits are rendered inoperative and tagged at every point where they can be energized. A sewer is different: OSHA says there is rarely any way to completely isolate a section of a continuous system (1910.146 Appendix E), so when isolation is infeasible the employer monitors continuously where entrants work and provides an early warning for engulfment (1926.1204(e)(1)). California: construction entries follow Title 8 section 1953(a)(3)(C) (isolating the permit space and physical hazards); general industry 5157(d)(3)(B) and (f)(8); and Cal/OSHA's lockout rule 3314: machinery stopped and its power source de-energized or disengaged (3314(c)) under a written hazardous energy control procedure (3314(g)). Plain-language summary, not the regulation; the regulation text and your company program govern.
